title: Chapter XXX

teacherSummary.text: Darcy and his cousin Colonel Fitzwilliam arrive at Rosings and promptly call at the parsonage. Fitzwilliam is pleasant and easy; Darcy is stiff and quiet. Charlotte guesses the visit is a compliment to Elizabeth.

vocabulary.definition: A part corresponding to another part
vocabulary.context: The entertainment of dining at Rosings was repeated about twice a week; and, allowing for the loss of Sir William, and there being only one card table in the evening, every such entertainment was the counterpart of the first.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “counterpart”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Younger sons like Fitzwilliam could not inherit and needed to marry money.

significance: Darcy's repeated visits show his feelings while Elizabeth misreads them.
discussionQuestions: Why does Darcy visit the parsonage so often?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with women's limited choices?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XXX,” how does Austen show Darcy at Rosings? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XXX, how does Austen develop the idea of Darcy at Rosings? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XXX develops the idea of Darcy at Rosings. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XXX (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Darcy at Rosings. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XXX suggests about Darcy at Rosings. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and irony), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XXX to complicate the reader's understanding of Darcy at Rosings. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XXX within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of Darcy at Rosings responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XXX alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of Darcy at Rosings follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XXX and its treatment of Darcy at Rosings. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and irony, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XXX as evidence for a larger claim about Darcy at Rosings in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XXX as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of Darcy at Rosings. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: From the drawing-room they could distinguish nothing in the lane, and were indebted to Mr. Collins for the knowledge of what carriages went along, and how often especially Miss de Bourgh drove by in her phaeton, which he never failed coming to inform them of, though it happened almost every day. She not unfrequently stopped at the Parsonage, and had a few minutes’ conversation with Charlotte, but was scarcely ever prevailed on to get out.

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

annotationFocus.label: Plot
annotationFocus.lookFor: key events and the causes linking them

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Why does Darcy visit the parsonage so often? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are counterpart, nephews, sallied, indebted, possessing. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “The entertainment of dining at Rosings was repeated about twice a week; and, allowing for the loss of Sir William, and there being only one card table in the evening, every such entertainment was the counterpart of the first.” Webster's says: A part corresponding to another part. Now the word history: “counterpart”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “nephew”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “sally”: -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Younger sons like Fitzwilliam could not inherit and needed to marry money. Why does this chapter matter? Darcy's repeated visits show his feelings while Elizabeth misreads them. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to Darcy at Rosings.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Plot.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: From the drawing-room they could distinguish nothing in the lane, and were indebted to Mr. Collins for the knowledge of what carriages went along, and how often especially Miss de Bourgh drove by in her phaeton, which he never failed coming to inform them of, though it happened almost every day. She not unfrequently stopped at the Parsonage, and had a few minutes’ conversation with Charlotte, but was scarcely ever prevailed on to get out.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Irony, Plot: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XXX,” how does Austen show Darcy at Rosings? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about Darcy at Rosings, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes Darcy at Rosings. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
